newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Thyssen on course despite Q1 sales fall.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Thyssen on course despite Q1 sales fall.

text.p: German steel and engineering group Thyssen AG said on Monday it had seen a poor start to the 1996/97 business year, with a six-percent fall in turnover, but expected a pickup over the full year.
Chief executive Dieter Vogel told Thyssen's annual news conference the group was on course for the full business year despite the group's poor first quarter.

"We expect the uptrend to resume after the traditionally weak first quarter," Vogel said. He said a restructuring plan adopted at Thyssen last November would be one of the main agents in turning the company around.

The restructuring plan would boost turnover, he said. Sales of 45 billion marks ($27.48 billion) by the end of the century were a realistic possibility, although Vogel did not rule out a possible dip in sales along the way.
In the year to the end of September 1996 sales were 38.7 billion marks.
The group plans to focus on its five core production areas of flat steel, elevator manufacturing, car parts, production systems and materials trading.
Five "potential" core production areas were also indentified -- construction technology, real estate, industrial services, logistics and telecommunications.
Thyssen is currently divided into three industrial divisions -- Thyssen Stahl AG, Thyssen Industrie AG and Thyssen Handel AG.
All three business divisions achieved positive operating results, but turnover was down six percent compared with the same quarter a year earlier at 8.7 billion marks.
Vogel said disposals had knocked 570 million marks off turnover in the first quarter, which began in October. On a comparable basis, turnover was flat on a year earlier, he said.

Steps had already been taken to dispose of non-core operations with annual turnover of some 2.8 billion marks and the group was considering options ranging from sales, cooperation deals and closure for 15 of its business areas.
Vogel ruled out a possible merger between Thyssen and fellow steelmaker Krupp-Hoesch, saying: "There are currently no discussions or negotiations on a possible merger or stake purchases going on."
He went on to say that the groups were in contact on shared areas of production, such as in the stainless steel area through their common holdings in the KTN unit.

One area of group activity which has been much in the news of late has been Thyssen's involvement in the building of Germany's multi-billion-mark Transrapid high-speed train, which analysts are increasingly concerned may be not be viable.
Thyssen said it would decide in the next two months on the project's future.

The high-tech magnetic levitation train, which is planned to run between Hamburg and Berlin from 2005, would now have to work on the basis of lower passenger income than previously anticipated, Vogel said.
Other partners in the project include Siemens AG and several large German construction companies.
The total cost of the project is officially estimated at nine billion marks, but critics charge it will inevitably cost a lot more.

On the payroll side, Thyssen's personnel director said the group planned to cut 8,700 jobs in 1996/97, which would mainly come from its domestic workforce. At the end of September 1996, Thyssen said it had nearly 127,000 employees, of which 96,815 were in Germany.
Net earnings per share (EPS) fell from 24 marks to 16 marks in 1995/96, while cash flow per share, calculated by the DVFA method, fell to 68 marks from 89 marks per share.
